l: mercy, Psalms
s: Mercy is what the speakers wait for from the LORD, looking to him until he grants it. They ask for it twice in verse 3, grounding the request in the contempt they have endured.

l: men (those who rose up against us), Psalms
s: Men rose up against the speakers, and their wrath was kindled against them. Had the LORD not been on the speakers' side, these men would have swallowed them alive, but they were not allowed to make the speakers their prey. The speakers escaped and the snare was broken.

l: the righteous, Psalms
s: The righteous are a group holding an allotment that wickedness's scepter will not rule, keeping their hands from evil; the psalmist closes by asking the LORD to do good to the upright.

l: the wicked (workers of iniquity), Psalms
s: turns_away_to crooked ways [habitual disposition] Those who turn away to their crooked ways will be led away by the LORD together with the workers of iniquity. The scepter of wickedness will not remain over the allotment of the righteous.

l: those who returned to Zion, Psalms
s: A group brought back to Zion by the LORD; they feel like dreamers, filled with laughter and singing, and the nations acknowledge the LORD's great deeds for them.

l: restoration of fortunes, Psalms
s: is_compared_to streams in the Negev [requested of the LORD] The restoration of fortunes is the subject of a petition asking the LORD to restore them again, like the streams in the Negev. It is set against the earlier return to Zion, which the speakers remember as a great deed of the LORD.

l: those who sow in tears, Psalms
s: will_reap_in joy [future outcome] Those who sow in tears are promised that they will reap in joy. The one who goes out weeping carrying seed for sowing will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.

l: children, Psalms
s: Children are portrayed in Chapter 127 as a heritage and reward from the LORD, the fruit of the womb, likened to arrows in a mighty man's hand; a man with a full quiver of them is happy.

l: man (who has a full quiver), Psalms
s: A man whose quiver is full of children is declared happy; he and his children are not disappointed when speaking with enemies in the gate.

l: vain labor and toil, Psalms
s: is_a futile [rising early and staying up late, eating the bread of toil] Building the house and guarding the city are in vain unless the LORD builds and watches. Rising early, staying up late, and eating the bread of toil are likewise called vain, since the LORD gives sleep to his loved ones.

l: everyone who fears the LORD, Psalms
s: The God-fearing person, described in Chapter 128, walks in the LORD's ways and is called blessed. He eats the labor of his hands, with a wife like a fruitful vine and children like olive shoots around his table. The wish extends to seeing Jerusalem's good and his children's children.

l: blessing, Psalms
s: Blessing is pronounced on everyone who fears the LORD and is described as enjoying the fruit of one's labor, happiness, well-being, and a flourishing household. It is also expressed as a wish: that the LORD bless the reader out of Zion, that he see the good of Jerusalem all his days, and that he see his children's children.

l: afflicters (those who afflicted Israel), Psalms
s: They have afflicted Israel many times from its youth up, plowing its back with long furrows. They have not prevailed against Israel.

l: wicked (enemies of Israel), Psalms
s: The LORD has cut apart the cords of the wicked. They are pictured as being restrained or freed from their hold by this act.

l: haters of Zion, Psalms
s: hate Zion The psalm asks that they be disappointed and turned backward, and be like grass on the housetops that withers before it grows up. Reapers and sheaf-binders gain nothing from them, and passersby do not bless them in the LORD's name.

l: psalmist (speaker of Chapter 130), Psalms
s: The psalmist, speaker of Chapter 130, cries to the LORD from the depths, pleading to be heard. He waits and hopes in the LORD's word, longing more than watchmen for morning, and finally exhorts Israel to hope in the LORD.

l: forgiveness, Psalms
s: Forgiveness is said to be with the LORD, and the psalmist states that this is why he is feared. It answers the problem raised by the possibility of the LORD keeping a record of sins.

l: redemption, Psalms
s: Abundant redemption is said to be with the LORD, as a reason for Israel to hope in him. The chapter concludes that he will redeem Israel from all their sins.

l: speaker (author of the psalm), Psalms
s: The speaker, identified as David, is a humble psalmist addressing the LORD. He disclaims arrogance, lofty eyes, and pursuit of great or wonderful matters beyond him. He describes his soul as stilled and quieted, like a weaned child with its mother, and ends by urging Israel to hope in the LORD.

l: weaned child (the speaker's simile), Psalms
s: The weaned child, shown with its mother, is the image the speaker uses for his stilled and quieted soul. The comparison is stated twice in verse 2: his soul is like a weaned child within him.

l: David's descendants (David's children), Psalms
s: The LORD promises to set the fruit of David's body on his throne. If David's children keep the LORD's covenant and the testimony he will teach them, their children will also sit on the throne forevermore.

l: David's vow, Psalms
s: has_content find a dwelling place for the LORD [no rest or sleep until fulfilled] David swore and vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob that he would not enter his house, go up into his bed, or give sleep to his eyes or slumber to his eyelids. He would not rest until he found a place for the LORD, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob.

l: dwelling place (the LORD's dwelling), Psalms
s: David vowed to find a place for the LORD, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob. The people heard of it in Ephrathah, found it in the field of Jaar, and resolve to go into his dwelling place and worship at his footstool. The LORD later declares Zion his resting place forever, where he will live because he desired it.

l: brothers, Psalms
s: live_in unity [described as good and pleasant] Brothers are described as living together in unity, which the speaker calls good and pleasant. Their shared life is the subject the whole chapter praises.

l: unity, Psalms
s: is_characteristic_of brothers [living together] Unity among brothers is declared both good and pleasant. It is illustrated by two images, the precious oil on Aaron's head and the dew of Hermon on Zion's hills.

l: precious oil (on Aaron's head), Psalms
s: Precious oil poured on Aaron's head runs down his beard to his robes' edge, serving as the first simile illustrating the goodness of brothers living together in unity.

l: dew of Hermon, Psalms
s: Dew of Hermon, which descends on the hills of Zion, serves as the second comparison illustrating the pleasantness of brothers living together in unity.

l: blessing, Psalms
s: is life forevermore The blessing is given by the LORD there on the hills of Zion. It is identified as life forevermore.

l: the LORD’s house, Psalms
s: The LORD's house is the place where the servants of the LORD stand by night. It is also referred to as the sanctuary, where hands are to be lifted in praise.

l: loving kindness (the LORD's), Psalms
s: duration forever [belongs to the LORD] God's loving kindness is declared to endure forever in the refrain that ends every one of the chapter's 26 verses. It is tied to his acts as creator, deliverer, giver of land, rememberer of the lowly and provider of food.

l: children of Edom, Psalms
s: urged_destruction_of Jerusalem [on the day of Jerusalem] The children of Edom are accused of saying 'Raze it! Raze it even to its foundation!' on the day of Jerusalem. The speaker asks the LORD to remember this against them.

l: Daughter of Babylon, Psalms
s: Daughter of Babylon, addressed as doomed to destruction for harming the exiles; the speaker blesses whoever repays her in kind, including dashing her little ones against the rock.

l: captives (exiles of Babylon), Psalms
s: Exiled captives in Babylon sit by the rivers weeping for Zion, hang their harps on willows, and ask how they can sing the LORD's song in a foreign land.

l: captors (those who led us captive), Psalms
s: Captors who held the Babylonian exiles captive and tormented them, finally mocking them by demanding joyful songs of Zion.

l: songs of Zion, Psalms
s: Songs of Zion are songs of joy that captors demand exiles sing for amusement; the exiles hang up their harps, asking how they can sing the LORD's song in a foreign land.

l: kings of the earth, Psalms
s: The kings of the earth, having heard the words of the LORD's mouth, will give thanks to him and sing of his ways because his glory is great.

l: the wicked (enemies of God), Psalms
s: The wicked are bloodthirsty enemies who speak wickedly against God and take his name in vain; David asks God to kill them, bids them depart, and hates them perfectly.

l: God's omniscience and omnipresence, Psalms
s: God's omniscience and omnipresence, as portrayed in Chapter 139: the LORD knows all of David's actions, thoughts, ways and words, and is present in heaven, Sheol, the farthest sea and darkness, a knowledge too lofty for David to grasp.

l: evil men (David's enemies), Psalms
s: A group of violent, proud evil men who are David's enemies. They plot mischief in their hearts, gather continually for war, and wield tongues sharpened like serpents with viper's poison under their lips. They hide snares, nets, and traps for the speaker's feet. The speaker prays their mischief will cover them with coals, fire, and pits; evil will hunt and overthrow them.

l: speaker (the psalmist), Psalms
s: The psalmist, identified as David, urgently calls on the LORD and asks to be guarded in speech and heart. He refuses fellowship with evildoers, welcomes righteous reproof, takes refuge in the LORD, and hopes the wicked fall into their own nets while he passes safely.

l: workers of iniquity, Psalms
s: The workers of iniquity are wicked people who practice wickedness and lay snares and traps for the psalmist, who refuses their delicacies and prays they fall together into their own nets while he passes safely.

l: righteous one, Psalms
s: strikes_speaker_as kindness [requested; reproof compared to oil on the head] The righteous one is described as striking and reproving the psalmist, which the psalmist says would be kindness and like oil on the head. The psalmist asks that his head not refuse it.

l: prayer (the psalmist's prayer), Psalms
s: The psalmist's prayer, asked to rise before the LORD like incense and evening sacrifice, and which he declares is always set against evil deeds.

l: persecutors (David's persecutors), Psalms
s: David's persecutors are described as too strong for him. They have hidden a snare for him on the path he walks, and he asks the LORD to deliver him from them.

l: enemy (David's enemy), Psalms
s: The enemy pursues David's soul and has struck his life down to the ground. He has made David live in dark places like those long dead. David asks the LORD to deliver him from his enemies, cut them off, and destroy all who afflict his soul.

l: prayer (David's prayer), Psalms
s: David's prayer opens with a plea that the LORD hear his petitions and relieve him, and it continues through requests for a quick answer, deliverance, guidance, and revival. It includes spreading out his hands and a soul thirsting like parched land. It ends with a request that the LORD cut off his enemies, based on David being God's servant.

l: foreigners, Psalms
s: Foreigners are deceitful people, mouths speaking lies and right hands of falsehood, from whom David repeatedly begs the LORD to rescue him.

l: prosperity of the people, Psalms
s: Prosperity of the people is a topic in Chapter 144 depicting a flourishing community: thriving sons and daughters, full barns, flocks of thousands and ten thousands, strong oxen, and security with no breaking in or outcry in the streets. Such people are called happy, chiefly because their God is the LORD.

l: saints, Psalms
s: The saints of the LORD, in Chapter 145, extol him and his works, then speak of his kingdom's glory and power, making his mighty acts known to humanity.

l: praise, Psalms
s: Praise is due to the LORD forever and ever, expressed in a psalm of David: he vows daily, eternal praise and meditation on God's greatness, generations and saints join in, and he ends calling all flesh to bless.

l: speaker (psalmist), Psalms
s: The psalmist urges his own soul to praise the LORD and vows lifelong praise and song. He warns against trusting princes, blesses those whose help and hope rest in the LORD, the God of Jacob, and ends by calling for praise.

l: princes, Psalms
s: Princes are warned against as objects of trust: being mere mortal sons of man who offer no help, their spirit departs, they return to earth, and their thoughts perish that day.

l: those who fear him (the LORD's favored), Psalms
s: The LORD takes pleasure in those who fear him and in those who hope in his loving kindness. Their favored status is set against his lack of delight in the strength of the horse or the legs of a man.

l: weather (the LORD's control of clouds, rain, snow, frost, hail, wind), Psalms
s: The LORD covers the sky with clouds, prepares rain for the earth, and makes grass grow on the mountains. He gives snow like wool, scatters frost like ashes, and hurls down hail like pebbles, so that no one can stand before his cold. He then melts them by sending out his word and causing his wind to blow so that the waters flow.

l: word of the LORD, Psalms
s: The LORD's word is his commandment going swiftly through the earth, melting snow, frost and hail, and revealed with statutes and ordinances to Jacob and Israel.

l: praise, Psalms
s: is good, pleasant and fitting [praising God] The psalm opens and closes with the call to praise the LORD, saying it is good, pleasant, and fitting. It urges singing with thanksgiving and praises on the harp, and directs Jerusalem and Zion to praise their God.

l: heavens, Psalms
s: The heavens are called to praise the LORD, along with angels, his army, sun, moon, shining stars, and the waters above them. They were created at his command and established forever and ever under a decree that will not pass away. His glory is said to be above them.

l: earth, Psalms
s: The earth is called to praise the LORD through sea creatures, depths, lightning, hail, snow, clouds, stormy wind, mountains, hills, trees, wild and domestic animals, birds, kings, peoples, princes, judges, and people of all ages. The stormy wind is described as fulfilling his word. His glory is said to be above the earth.

l: praise of the LORD, Psalms
s: Praise of the LORD is a repeated command, opening and closing chapters 148 and 149 with 'Praise the LORD!'. Chapter 148 summons heavens and earth to praise his name, because he created all things by command and his name alone is exalted. Chapter 149 directs it to the saints' assembly, with a new song, dance, tambourine, harp.

l: saints, Psalms
s: The saints are the people of the LORD, a group honored by God. They gather in the assembly of the new song, rejoicing and singing for joy on their beds. With high praises in their mouths and two-edged swords in their hands, they execute vengeance and punishments on nations, binding kings with chains and nobles with iron fetters.

l: nations, Psalms
s: The nations, with their peoples, are targets of vengeance and punishment by the saints; their kings are bound in chains and nobles in iron fetters as the written judgment is executed.

l: vengeance and punishments, Psalms
s: Vengeance and punishments are to be executed on the nations and peoples by the saints, who hold a two-edged sword. They include binding kings with chains and nobles with iron fetters, carrying out the written judgment, which is called an honor for all his saints.

l: everything that has breath, Psalms
s: is_called_to praise [directed at the LORD] Everything that has breath is called on in the final verse to praise the LORD. This universal summons ends the chapter.

l: praise, Psalms
s: is_directed_to the LORD Praise is commanded repeatedly throughout the chapter, directed at the LORD in his sanctuary and heavens and for his acts of power, mighty acts, and greatness. It is to be expressed with trumpet, harp, lyre, tambourine, dancing, stringed instruments, flute, and loud, resounding cymbals. The chapter closes by extending it to everything that has breath.

l: The Gospel According to John
s: This is the Gospel According to John, chapters 1 to 21, a narrative of the life, teaching, death and resurrection of Jesus, centered on his identity as the Word made flesh, the Son of God and the Christ. The most important figures are Jesus, John (the witness who baptizes), Simon Peter, Judas Iscariot, Thomas, Nicodemus, Mary Magdalene, Pilate, and the disciple whom Jesus loved, who is named at the close as the witness who wrote these things. Chapter 1 opens with the Word who was with God and was God, then John's testimony that Jesus is the Lamb of God, and the calling of Andrew, Peter, Philip and Nathanael. Chapters 2 to 4 present early signs and encounters: water turned to wine at Cana, the temple cleansing, Nicodemus told he must be born anew, the Samaritan woman at the well, and the healing of a nobleman's son. Chapters 5 to 10 show escalating conflict with the Jews. Jesus heals on the Sabbath, feeds five thousand, walks on water, and declares himself the bread of life, the light of the world, the door and the good shepherd. Many disciples turn back, Peter confesses him as the Christ, and he says 'before Abraham came into existence, I AM' and 'I and the Father are one.' Crowds divide, a blind man is healed, and attempts to stone or seize Jesus recur. Chapter 11 brings the raising of Lazarus, after which the chief priests and Pharisees, with Caiaphas speaking, resolve to kill Jesus. Chapter 12 has Mary anointing him, the entry into Jerusalem, and his warning to walk in the light. Chapters 13 to 17 take place with the disciples before the Passover. Jesus washes their feet, identifies Judas as the betrayer, gives a new commandment to love one another, and foretells Peter's denial. He comforts them as the way, the truth and the life, promises the Counselor, the Spirit of truth, calls himself the true vine, warns of persecution, and prays for his disciples and future believers to be one. Chapters 18 and 19 recount the arrest in the garden, Peter's three denials, the trial before Pilate, the flogging, the demand for crucifixion, the death at Golgotha with 'It is finished,' and the burial by Joseph of Arimathaea and Nicodemus. Chapter 20 tells of the empty tomb, Mary Magdalene meeting the risen Jesus, his appearance to the disciples, and Thomas declaring 'My Lord and my God!' Chapter 21 closes with Jesus appearing at the sea of Tiberias, the large catch of fish, breakfast on the beach, and Peter's three-fold commissioning to feed his sheep.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to John
s: Jesus is the central figure of these records from the Gospel According to John: the Word who was with God in the beginning, became flesh, and is full of grace and truth. He is presented as the only born Son of God, sent by the Father, who came down from heaven and is one with the Father. He is also called Lamb of God, King of Israel, Christ, Teacher, Lord, Savior of the world and Son of Man. He is a Jew from Nazareth, called the son of Joseph, with a mother, brothers and disciples. What matters most is his relationship to the Father: he does what pleases the Father, speaks by the Father's commandment, holds authority over judgment and life, and reveals the Father. He describes himself as the bread of life, light of the world, door, good shepherd, resurrection and life, the way, truth and life, and the true vine. The account begins with John's testimony and the calling of disciples, then moves through the wedding at Cana, the cleansing of the temple, and teaching Nicodemus and a Samaritan woman. Signs and conflict follow: healings, feeding the multitude, walking on the sea, and the claim 'before Abraham existed, I AM.' The Jews seek to kill him, and he withdraws and avoids Judea. He gives sight to a blind man, declares he lays down his life and takes it again, and raises Lazarus. The council then resolves to kill him. He enters Jerusalem on a donkey, hailed as King of Israel. With his disciples he washes their feet, gives a new commandment of love, predicts betrayal and Peter's denial, promises the Counselor, says he has overcome the world, and prays for them. In the garden he is seized and bound, questioned, and brought before Pilate, saying his Kingdom is not of this world. He is crucified as King of the Jews, entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple, says 'It is finished,' and is buried. He rises, appears to Mary Magdalene, the disciples and Thomas, gives the Holy Spirit, and at the sea of Tiberias feeds his disciples and commissions Peter to feed his sheep.

l: God, The Gospel According to John
s: In these records, God is portrayed in The Gospel According to John as the Father of Jesus, the sender of the Son, and the source of life, love, judgment, and glory. Early on, God is the one with whom the Word was in the beginning; no one has seen him, though the only born Son has declared him. He sent John to baptize, and those who receive and believe the Word are given the right to become his children. He so loved the world that he gave his only born Son so the world would be saved, not judged, and he gives the Spirit without measure. His wrath remains on those who disobey the Son. As the account unfolds, the Father is shown loving the Son, showing him all he does, raising the dead and giving them life, and having life in himself, which he gave the Son too. He gave all judgment and all things into the Son's hands, and has testified about Jesus, though the Jews have never heard his voice or seen his form. Jesus' works reveal God's works, and his illness-healings and Lazarus' sickness serve God's glory. People debate whether God listens to sinners or to worshipers who do his will. The Father always listens to Jesus, and a voice from the sky confirms that he has glorified his name and will do so again. He gave Jesus a commandment that is eternal life, and whoever receives or sees Jesus receives or sees the one who sent him. In the later chapters, the Father is the farmer of the true vine, pruning branches and being glorified when disciples bear fruit. He loves the disciples because they loved Jesus, gives whatever they ask in Jesus' name, and is with Jesus. The Spirit of truth proceeds from him. In the final prayer he is addressed as Holy and Righteous Father, the only true God, who gave Jesus authority over all flesh and the disciples out of the world, and who loved Jesus before the foundation of the world. Jesus asks him to glorify the Son and to keep and sanctify the disciples.

l: John, The Gospel According to John
s: John is a man sent from God as a witness to testify about the light, though he is not the light himself. He denies being the Christ, Elijah, or the prophet, and calls himself the voice crying in the wilderness. He baptizes in water, first at Bethany beyond the Jordan and later at Enon near Salim. He testifies that Jesus is the Lamb of God and Son of God, and two of his disciples follow Jesus. When his disciples complain that everyone is going to Jesus, John calls himself the bridegroom's friend and declares, 'He must increase, but I must decrease.'

l: Andrew, The Gospel According to John
s: Andrew, from Bethsaida and brother of Simon Peter, was a disciple of John who followed Jesus after hearing him called the Lamb of God, stayed with him, then told Simon they found the Messiah and brought him.

l: Simon Peter, The Gospel According to John
s: Simon Peter, son of Jonah and brother of Andrew, is a disciple of Jesus from Bethsaida and one of the twelve. Brought to Jesus by Andrew in Chapter 1, he is renamed Cephas, interpreted Peter. In Chapter 6 he speaks for the twelve, confessing Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God, and saying they have nowhere else to go. In Chapter 13 he first objects to having his feet washed, then asks for more washing, and vows to lay down his life for Jesus, who predicts he will deny him three times. In Chapter 18 he draws a sword and cuts off Malchus's right ear, is told to sheathe it, and then in the high priest's court denies being a disciple three times, the last followed by a rooster crowing. In Chapter 20 he is outrun to the tomb but is first to enter and sees the linen cloths. In Chapter 21 he proposes fishing, throws himself into the sea on recognizing the Lord, affirms his affection for Jesus when questioned three times, and is commissioned to feed and tend Jesus' lambs and sheep. Jesus signifies his death will glorify God and tells him to follow.

l: Philip, The Gospel According to John
s: Philip is a disciple of Jesus from Bethsaida of Galilee, the city of Andrew and Peter. Jesus finds him and says "Follow me." He brings Nathanael to Jesus, answering doubt with "Come and see." Later he asks Jesus to show them the Father, and Jesus replies that whoever has seen him has seen the Father.

l: Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, The Gospel According to John
s: Nathanael of Cana, an Israelite without deceit, is brought by Philip to Jesus of Nazareth. He doubts anything good comes from Nazareth, but after Jesus says he saw him under the fig tree, he declares Jesus Son of God and King of Israel.

l: the Jews, The Gospel According to John
s: The Jews appear in these records as a collective antagonist group whose relationship with Jesus moves from questioning and misunderstanding to hostility and finally to delivering him for execution. They claim descent from Abraham and God as their Father, set their hope on Moses, search the Scriptures believing they hold eternal life, and meet always in the temple. Jesus says they lack God's love, that Moses accuses them, and that their father is the devil. They have agreed to expel from the synagogue anyone confessing Jesus as Christ, and they disbelieve because they are not of his sheep. Their central stance is a persistent desire to kill Jesus. The account begins at the temple, where they ask for a sign and misread his words about raising the temple as being about a building rather than his body. In Chapter 5 they object to a healed man carrying his mat on the Sabbath, then persecute Jesus and seek to kill him because he broke the Sabbath and called God his Father. In Chapter 6 they murmur at his claim to be the bread from heaven, pointing to his known parents, and argue among themselves. In Chapter 7 they look for him at the feast, marvel at his learning, and are so feared that no one speaks openly of him. In Chapter 8 many believe, but the group objects that they are Abraham's offspring, calls him a Samaritan with a demon, and takes up stones. In Chapter 9 they doubt the blind man's healing, question his parents, and declare Jesus a sinner. In Chapter 10 they are divided, press him to say if he is the Christ, and take up stones for blasphemy, claiming he, a man, makes himself God. In Chapter 11 some console Martha and Mary, and many who see Lazarus raised believe, while others report to the Pharisees. In Chapters 18 and 19 their officers seize and bind Jesus, take him to Annas and then Pilate, avoid defilement before Passover, state they may not put anyone to death, and choose Barabbas. They say by their law he must die for making himself the Son of God, press Pilate with the threat of Caesar, and ask that the crucified be removed before the Sabbath, after which Jesus is laid in a nearby tomb. Throughout, the group is divided in places, but its dominant force is opposition.

l: Pharisees, The Gospel According to John
s: The Pharisees are a group of religious authorities who consistently oppose Jesus across the records. Acting with the chief priests, they send officers to arrest him, dismiss the crowd as cursed for not knowing the law, and insist no ruler or Pharisee believes in him. They bring the woman taken in adultery to test him, then reject his self-testimony as invalid. In the healing episode they interrogate the healed man and his parents, split over whether Jesus can be from God since he healed on the Sabbath, claim to be disciples of Moses, and expel the man. Jesus tells them their sin remains because they claim to see. Finally, after a report of what Jesus did, they gather a council with the chief priests, fear everyone will believe in him, plan his death, and command that anyone knowing his whereabouts report it so he can be seized.

l: Galilee, The Gospel According to John
s: Galilee is Jesus' home region and contains Cana, where he made water into wine and later heals a nobleman's son. Galileans welcome him after seeing his deeds at the Jerusalem feast, though he notes a prophet lacks honor at home. He stays there to avoid Judea's threats, while Pharisees and some of the crowd dismiss it as no source of prophets or the Christ.

l: Holy Spirit, The Gospel According to John
s: The Holy Spirit is the Counselor and Spirit of truth, sent by the Father in Jesus' name and proceeding from the Father. In Chapter 14, he is promised to stay with and be in the disciples forever, unseen and unknown by the world, teaching all things and recalling Jesus' words. In Chapter 16, Jesus says he must depart first; then the Spirit convicts the world of sin, righteousness and judgment, guides disciples into all truth, declares coming things, and glorifies Jesus.

l: Mary (Jesus' mother), The Gospel According to John
s: Jesus' mother is a woman with a sister who appears at two moments. At the Cana wedding she tells Jesus they have no wine and instructs the servants to obey him, then travels to Capernaum with his family and disciples. At the cross, Jesus entrusts her to the disciple, who takes her home.

l: disciples (Jesus' disciples), The Gospel According to John
s: The disciples are the group of followers chosen and appointed by Jesus, taken out of the world to bear lasting fruit. They are first seen invited with Jesus to a wedding, where they believe in him after he reveals his glory. Their faith grows unevenly: they recall Scripture at the temple, and only after his resurrection do they fully believe the Scripture and his word. They baptize on his behalf, misunderstand his talk of food while he speaks with a woman, and are sent to reap what others labored for. They distribute loaves and fish and see him walk on water, yet many followers find his teaching hard and turn back while the twelve remain, including Judas, who would betray him. At the foot-washing they are told they are clean, except one. Jesus commands them to love one another so everyone will know they are his disciples. He promises a prepared place, the Counselor, and his peace, though Thomas, Philip, and Judas (not Iscariot) show incomplete understanding. He calls them branches who must remain in him, and friends rather than servants, warning of the world's hatred, persecution, expulsion, and death. They will testify because they have been with him from the beginning. They claim to believe because he speaks plainly, but he foretells they will scatter and leave him alone, promising their sorrow will become joy and that in him they may have peace.

l: wedding (in Cana of Galilee), The Gospel According to John
s: located_in Cana of Galilee The wedding takes place on the third day in Cana of Galilee, with Jesus, his mother, and his disciples present. When the wine runs out, Jesus provides wine, and the ruler of the feast calls the bridegroom and praises him for keeping the good wine until now.

l: wine, The Gospel According to John
s: The wine runs out at the wedding, prompting Jesus' mother to speak to him. Water drawn from the filled pots becomes wine, and the ruler of the feast, not knowing its source, calls it the good wine kept until now, better than what is usually served first.

l: water pots (at the wedding), The Gospel According to John
s: Six stone water pots, each holding two or three metretes, stand at the wedding for Jewish purifying; at Jesus' command servants fill them with water, and what is drawn out is wine.

l: brothers (Jesus' brothers), The Gospel According to John
s: is_disposed_toward unbelief in Jesus Jesus' brothers urge him to leave Galilee and go into Judea to show his works openly to the world. The text states that they did not believe in him. They go up to the feast ahead of him.

l: temple (in Jerusalem), The Gospel According to John
s: The temple in Jerusalem, which the Jews say took forty-six years to build and which includes Solomon's porch, is where Jesus at Passover drives out sellers and money-changers, calls it his Father's house, and speaks of raising it in three days, meaning his body.

l: sellers and money changers (in the temple), The Gospel According to John
s: located_in temple (in Jerusalem) [sold oxen, sheep, doves and changed money] Those selling oxen, sheep, and doves and the money changers sitting in the temple are driven out by Jesus with a whip of cords. He pours out the changers' money, overturns their tables, and tells the dove sellers to take their things away and not make his Father's house a marketplace.

l: temple cleansing, The Gospel According to John
s: Before Passover in the Jerusalem temple, Jesus whips out sellers and animals, scatters money and overturns tables; disciples recall a zeal scripture, and the Jews demand a sign from him.

l: signs of Jesus, The Gospel According to John
s: Signs of Jesus: begins with water turned to wine at Cana, revealing his glory and prompting disciples' belief; at Passover in Jerusalem many believe in his name from the signs, while the Jews demand a sign for cleansing the temple.

l: Nicodemus, The Gospel According to John
s: Nicodemus is a Pharisee and ruler of the Jews, addressed by Jesus as a teacher of Israel. In Chapter 3 he visits Jesus by night, calls him a teacher from God because of his signs, misunderstands being born anew, asks 'How can these things be?', and is rebuked for not understanding. In Chapter 7 he asks his fellow Pharisees whether the law judges a man without first hearing him, and they mock him as a Galilean. In Chapter 19 he brings about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes and helps bind Jesus' body in linen according to Jewish burial custom.

l: new birth, The Gospel According to John
s: New birth, of water and Spirit, is required to see and enter God's Kingdom. Jesus tells Nicodemus this, contrasting flesh-born with Spirit-born and likening the Spirit to unpredictable wind; Nicodemus takes it literally and fails to understand.

l: God's Kingdom, The Gospel According to John
s: God's Kingdom is something one can't see unless born anew and can't enter unless born of water and Spirit. It is mentioned in Jesus's first two statements to Nicodemus.

l: eternal life, The Gospel According to John
s: Eternal life is a gift received by whoever believes in Jesus, the Son, and is defined as knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ. It begins with a promise in Chapter 3 that believers will not perish, tied to the Son being lifted up. Chapter 6 adds food that remains, being raised at the last day, and Jesus' words of eternal life. Chapter 17 defines it and says Jesus gives it to those the Father gave him.

l: world, The Gospel According to John
s: The world is presented as the realm opposed to Jesus and his followers. It is ruled by a prince who has been judged, does not know the Father, cannot receive or know the Spirit of truth, and will see Jesus no more after a little while. It hated Jesus first, then hates the disciples because they are not of it, persecuting them out of ignorance of the one who sent Jesus. Having seen his works, it has no excuse for its sin. The account unfolds across four chapters: Chapter 14 states its inability to receive the Spirit and Jesus' coming departure from its sight; Chapter 15 describes its hatred as fulfilling scripture; Chapter 16 says the Counselor will convict it of sin, righteousness and judgment, that it will rejoice while the disciples weep, and that Jesus has overcome it though the disciples have trouble in it; Chapter 17 shows it as the realm the disciples came from and are sent into. Jesus does not pray for it, but asks that the disciples' unity lead it to believe.

l: judgment, The Gospel According to John
s: is_defined_as light has come into the world and men loved darkness [because their works were evil] Jesus says God did not send his Son to judge the world but to save it. The one who believes is not judged, while the one who doesn't believe has been judged already for not believing in the name of the only born Son. The judgment is that the light has come into the world and men loved the darkness because their works were evil.

l: light and darkness, The Gospel According to John
s: relates_to evil works [those who do evil hate the light] Light is said to have come into the world, but men loved darkness rather than light because their works were evil. Everyone who does evil hates the light and avoids it so his works are not exposed. The one who does the truth comes to the light so that his works may be revealed as done in God.

l: Samaritan woman, The Gospel According to John
s: A Samaritan woman with five former husbands, living with a man not her husband, meets Jesus at Jacob's well. Asked for a drink, she is surprised, then perceives him as a prophet, raises where to worship, and hears him declare he is the Messiah. She leaves her water pot, tells the city, and her testimony leads many to believe.

l: Samaritans, The Gospel According to John
s: The Samaritans live in Samaria and are shunned by Jews. Many from the city believe in Jesus through a woman's testimony, host him two days, and more believe his word, proclaiming him Savior of the world.

l: Jacob's well, The Gospel According to John
s: Jacob's well is a deep well at Sychar in Samaria, near ground Jacob gave Joseph. Jacob gave it to the woman's people and drank from it with his children and livestock. Jesus, tired, sits by it, and his conversation with the Samaritan woman occurs there.

l: living water, The Gospel According to John
s: Living water is a gift from Jesus, described in Chapter 4 to the Samaritan woman. Unlike ordinary water, which leaves one thirsty again, it ends thirst and becomes within the drinker a well springing up to eternal life. The woman responds by asking for it.

l: worship, The Gospel According to John
s: must_be in spirit and truth [true worshipers of the Father] The woman raises the dispute between worshiping on the Samaritan mountain and in Jerusalem. Jesus replies that the hour is coming, and now is, when neither place will matter and true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, since the Father seeks such worshipers and God is spirit. He also says the Samaritans worship what they do not know, while "we" worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews.

l: nobleman, The Gospel According to John
s: A nobleman whose son lies sick at Capernaum begs Jesus at Cana to heal him. Jesus says the son lives; the man believes his word and leaves. Servants report recovery, and the nobleman and his whole house come to believe.

l: nobleman's son, The Gospel According to John
s: A nobleman's son at Capernaum lies near death with fever; his father's servants report he lives, having begun recovering at the seventh hour, exactly when Jesus said "Your son lives."

l: healing of nobleman's son, The Gospel According to John
s: The second sign Jesus performed in Galilee after leaving Judea: from a distance, without going to Capernaum, he says "Your son lives"; the fever left at that very hour, and the father's whole house believes.

l: man healed at Bethesda (sick for thirty-eight years), The Gospel According to John
s: A man sick for thirty-eight years, with no one to help him into the pool, is instantly healed by Jesus at his command and walks carrying his mat. Not knowing his healer at first, he later learns and tells the Jews it was Jesus.

l: Bethesda, The Gospel According to John
s: Bethesda is a pool in Jerusalem by the sheep gate, with five porches, where many sick people waited for the angel-stirred water to heal the first in; it is where Jesus heals a man ill thirty-eight years.

l: Feast of Booths, The Gospel According to John
s: The Feast of Booths is a Jewish feast that frames Chapter 7: Jesus' brothers go up, Jesus follows secretly and teaches in the temple mid-feast, then on its greatest last day invites the thirsty.

l: Sabbath, The Gospel According to John
s: The Sabbath is the day Jesus heals the man at Bethesda. The Jews say carrying a mat is unlawful then, so they persecute Jesus and seek to kill him, angered that he broke it and called God his Father.

l: works of Jesus, The Gospel According to John
s: The works of Jesus are good deeds that originate from the Father, who gave them to him to accomplish. Done in the Father's name, they testify that the Father sent him. In chapter 10 he challenges the Jews' stoning, urging belief in the works so they know the Father is in him.

l: testimony about Jesus, The Gospel According to John
s: Testimony about Jesus: he says self-testimony alone would be invalid, so others witness for him, John, the works the Father gave him (greater than John's), the Father, and the Scriptures, yet the Jews disbelieve these witnesses and won't come to him for life.

l: resurrection and judgment, The Gospel According to John
s: is_destiny_of those who have done evil Jesus says the Father has given all judgment to the Son, who also gives life to whom he desires, and that those who hear his word and believe the one who sent him have eternal life and have passed out of death into life. He says the hour comes when all in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who did good to the resurrection of life and those who did evil to the resurrection of judgment. He says the Son has authority to execute judgment because he is a son of man, and that his own judgment is righteous.

l: Judas Iscariot, The Gospel According to John
s: Judas Iscariot, son of Simon, is one of the twelve disciples and the one who betrays Jesus. He keeps the money box and steals from it, and he objects to the costly ointment while caring nothing for the poor. At the meal the devil has put betrayal into his heart; Jesus gives him the dipped bread, Satan enters him, and he leaves into the night at Jesus's urging to act quickly. He then leads soldiers and officers with lanterns, torches, and weapons to the garden he knows, standing with them when Jesus identifies himself.

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Gospel According to John
s: The disciples are Jesus's followers, including Thomas called Didymus and Peter. At first they gather behind locked doors, afraid of the Jews. Jesus appears, gives peace, sends them as the Father sent him, breathes the Holy Spirit on them, and grants authority over forgiving and retaining sins. They tell Thomas they have seen the Lord, and Jesus appears again after eight days. Later, seven fish all night at the sea of Tiberias, catch nothing, obey Jesus, and share his breakfast.

l: multitude (following Jesus), The Gospel According to John
s: The great multitude follows Jesus because of his signs on the sick, is fed by him, and calls him the prophet who comes into the world. They intend to take him by force to make him king, then cross by boat to Capernaum seeking him. Jesus tells them they seek him for the loaves, not for the signs, and they ask for the bread he speaks of.

l: God the Father, The Gospel According to John
s: God the Father appears in these records as the sender of Jesus and the source of his authority. Early on, the Father sends and seals Jesus, gives the true bread from heaven, and draws and gives people to Jesus; no one comes unless the Father draws or grants it. Jesus came to do the Father's will, losing none of those given and raising them at the last day. Jesus says his teaching is not his own but the sender's, that the sender is true, that the crowd does not know him, and that Jesus will go to him. The Father is with Jesus, testifies about him, glorifies him, and teaches him what to speak, while Jesus always does what pleases him. The Jews claim him as Father but do not know him. The Father knows and loves Jesus because he lays down his life, commanded him to lay down and take up that life, and gave him sheep that no one can snatch from his hand. He is greater than all, and Jesus says 'I and the Father are one,' that the Father sanctified and sent him, and later that the Father is greater than he. Finally, the Father dwells in Jesus, works through him, will give another Counselor, loves those who love Jesus, and will make a home with them.

l: sea of Tiberias, The Gospel According to John
s: also_called Sea of Tiberias Jesus goes to the other side of the sea of Galilee, also called the Sea of Tiberias. A great wind tosses the sea as the disciples row across it, and they see Jesus walking on it.

l: feeding of the five thousand, The Gospel According to John
s: has_size about five thousand men At Passover time Jesus asks Philip where to buy bread, to test him, and has the people sit on the grass. About five thousand men are fed, and the multitude then calls him the prophet who comes into the world. Jesus afterward says the multitude seeks him because they ate and were filled.

l: loaves and fish, The Gospel According to John
s: consists_of five barley loaves and two fish [belonging to the boy] A boy's five barley loaves and two fish, which Andrew says are little among so many, are taken by Jesus, who gives thanks and distributes them. All eat as much as they desire, and twelve baskets of broken pieces are left from the loaves.

l: Jesus walking on the sea, The Gospel According to John
s: At night, after rowing about twenty-five or thirty stadia, the disciples see Jesus walking on the sea and drawing near the boat, and they are afraid. He tells them "It is I. Don't be afraid," and immediately the boat is at the land where they were going.

l: manna, The Gospel According to John
s: was_eaten_by Jews' fathers [in the wilderness; they died] The multitude cites the manna their fathers ate in the wilderness as a sign, quoting that God gave them bread out of heaven. Jesus replies that Moses did not give it, that the Father gives the true bread, and that the fathers ate manna and died.

l: bread of life discourse (true bread from heaven), The Gospel According to John
s: In the synagogue at Capernaum Jesus says he is the bread of life and the living bread that came down from heaven, and that whoever comes to and believes in him will not hunger or thirst. The teaching about eating his flesh divides his hearers, leading to murmuring, contention, and many disciples departing.

l: Jesus's flesh and blood, The Gospel According to John
s: Jesus's flesh and blood are described as true food and drink that give eternal life to those who eat and drink them. Jesus says the bread he gives for the world's life is his flesh; the Jews question how, and many disciples find it hard.

l: belief in Jesus, The Gospel According to John
s: Belief in Jesus is described as the work of God and gives eternal life and lasting satisfaction. Some who saw him disbelieve, since coming requires the Father's gift; many disciples leave, but Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, Son of the living God.

l: the multitude, The Gospel According to John
s: A crowd, deemed ignorant of the law by the Pharisees, murmurs about Jesus in Chapter 7. Opinions split: good man versus deceiver, demon-possessed, prophet, or Christ, while some object over Galilee; many believe because of his signs.

l: the chief priests, The Gospel According to John
s: The chief priests act as a group aligned with the Pharisees against Jesus. In Chapter 7 they send officers to arrest him and question them when they return empty-handed. In Chapter 11 they convene a council, fearing Roman reprisal, resolve to kill him, order his whereabouts reported, and plot against Lazarus.

l: officers (sent by the chief priests and Pharisees), The Gospel According to John
s: regards_jesus_as unequaled speaker The officers are sent to arrest Jesus but return without him. They explain to the chief priests and Pharisees, "No man ever spoke like this man!"

l: woman taken in adultery, The Gospel According to John
s: A woman accused of adultery, said to be caught in the act, is brought by scribes and Pharisees and set in the middle. Her accusers leave one by one; Jesus does not condemn her and tells her to go and sin no more.

l: Abraham, The Gospel According to John
s: Abraham is a deceased figure whom the Jews claim as their father. Jesus contrasts their conduct with Abraham's works, says Abraham rejoiced to see his day, and declares he existed before Abraham; the Jews counter that Abraham died.

l: the devil, The Gospel According to John
s: The devil is described by Jesus in Chapter 8 as a murderer from the beginning, without truth, who speaks lies from his own nature, a liar and father of lies, whose desires the Jews want to do.

l: stoning of the woman, The Gospel According to John
s: is_commanded_by Moses [in the law, for such women] The scribes and Pharisees cite Moses' command to stone such women and ask Jesus what he says. Jesus says the one without sin should throw the first stone, and the accusers leave one by one, oldest first, so the stoning does not happen. Later, the Jews take up stones to throw at Jesus himself, but he escapes.

l: sin, The Gospel According to John
s: enslaves everyone who commits sin [bondservant of sin] Jesus says the one without sin may throw the first stone, and tells the woman to sin no more. He says that those who do not believe he is he will die in their sins, and that everyone who commits sin is a bondservant of sin. He asks which of his accusers convicts him of sin.

l: truth and freedom, The Gospel According to John
s: is_gained_by remaining in Jesus' word [disciples know the truth and are made free] Jesus tells those who believed him that if they remain in his word they will know the truth and the truth will make them free. They protest that they have never been in bondage, and he answers that everyone who commits sin is sin's bondservant, a bondservant does not remain in the house forever, and if the Son makes them free they will be free indeed. He says he tells the truth, which they do not believe, while the devil has no truth in him.

l: blind man (healed by Jesus), The Gospel According to John
s: A beggar blind from birth is healed after washing at Siloam as Jesus directed. He affirms his identity to doubting neighbors, then under repeated Pharisee questioning calls Jesus a prophet, says he knows only that he now sees, and argues Jesus is from God. Expelled by the Pharisees, he comes to believe in Jesus as Lord and worships him.

l: parents (the blind man's parents), The Gospel According to John
s: The parents are asked whether the man is their son and whether he was born blind, and they confirm both. They say they don't know how he now sees or who opened his eyes, and tell the questioners to ask him since he is of age. The text says they answer this way because they fear the Jews and expulsion from the synagogue.

l: pool of Siloam, The Gospel According to John
s: means Sent [translation of name] Jesus sends the blind man to wash in the pool of Siloam, a name explained as meaning "Sent." The man goes, washes, and returns seeing, and he later cites the pool in telling others how he received his sight.

l: mud (Jesus' mud), The Gospel According to John
s: Jesus spits on the ground, makes mud with the saliva, and anoints the blind man's eyes with it. The man later describes this to neighbors and Pharisees as how Jesus opened his eyes, and the making of mud is noted as having occurred on a Sabbath.

l: healing of the blind man, The Gospel According to John
s: A man blind from birth is given sight on a Sabbath when Jesus anoints his eyes with mud and he washes at Siloam, meant to reveal God's works. It sparks neighbor disputes, divides the Pharisees, and the man calls it unprecedented.

l: blindness and sight (spiritual), The Gospel According to John
s: has_consequence sin remains for those who claim to see [Jesus' teaching] Jesus says he came into the world for judgment so that those who don't see may see and those who see may become blind. When the Pharisees ask if they are also blind, he answers that if they were blind they would have no sin, but because they say they see, their sin remains. The physically blind man gains sight and also comes to belief, while the Pharisees who claim to see are rebuked.

l: sheep (Jesus' sheep), The Gospel According to John
s: Jesus' sheep are his followers who recognize his voice, are called by name, and follow him while fleeing strangers. They receive eternal life and cannot be snatched from his or the Father's hand. Other sheep will join them as one flock; unbelieving Jews are not his sheep.

l: shepherd (in the parable), The Gospel According to John
s: The shepherd in Jesus' parable enters the sheep fold by the door, is admitted by the gatekeeper, calls his sheep by name and leads them out ahead. He contrasts with thieves and hired hands; Jesus later identifies himself as the good shepherd.

l: the good shepherd parable, The Gospel According to John
s: is_a parable [spoken by Jesus] Jesus speaks the sheep fold parable in verses 1-5, and those listening do not understand it. He then explains it in two images: he is the door through which one is saved and finds pasture, and he is the good shepherd who knows his own and lays down his life, unlike the thief or the hired hand. The thief comes to steal, kill and destroy, while Jesus came that the sheep may have life abundantly.

l: Jesus' death and resurrection, The Gospel According to John
s: Jesus says repeatedly that he lays down his life for the sheep. He states that the Father loves him because he lays down his life that he may take it again, that no one takes it from him, and that he has power to lay it down and take it up by the Father's commandment.

l: blasphemy, The Gospel According to John
s: The Jews say they stone Jesus not for a good work but for blasphemy, because he, being a man, makes himself God. Jesus answers that the law calls those to whom God's word came 'gods' and asks why they say he blasphemes for saying he is the Son of God, whom the Father sanctified and sent.

l: Lazarus, The Gospel According to John
s: Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Mary and loved by Jesus, falls sick and dies. After four days in the tomb, Jesus calls him out, still wrapped in grave cloths, and orders him freed. Later he dines with Jesus at the supper in Bethany. Crowds come to see him, and the chief priests plot to kill him because many believed in Jesus through him.

l: Martha, The Gospel According to John
s: Martha is a woman, sister of Mary and Lazarus, who serves the supper at Bethany. When Lazarus falls sick she sends word to Jesus, meets him, confesses him as Christ and God's Son, calls Mary secretly, and objects at the tomb until reminded about belief.

l: Mary, The Gospel According to John
s: Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus, is known for anointing Jesus' feet with ointment and wiping them with her hair. In Chapter 11 she grieves Lazarus's death, falling at Jesus' feet and troubling him with her weeping. In Chapter 12 she anoints him with costly nard, and Jesus defends her against Judas, saying it prepares for his burial.

l: Thomas, The Gospel According to John
s: Thomas, also called Didymus, is one of the twelve disciples of Jesus. In Chapter 14 he asks how they can know the way, prompting Jesus to call himself the way, truth, and life. In Chapter 20, absent at first, he doubts the others' report until Jesus appears and he declares 'My Lord and my God!'

l: Caiaphas, The Gospel According to John
s: Caiaphas is the high priest that year and son-in-law of Annas. He tells the council it is advantageous for one man to die for the people so the nation does not perish; the text calls this prophecy that Jesus would die for the nation and gather God's scattered children. Later, Annas sends the bound Jesus to him, and from his house Jesus is led to the Praetorium.

l: Bethany, The Gospel According to John
s: located_near Jerusalem [about fifteen stadia away] Bethany is the village of Mary and Martha and the home of Lazarus. It is near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away, and many of the Jews gather there to console the sisters.

l: tomb (Lazarus's tomb), The Gospel According to John
s: Lazarus's tomb is a cave with a stone lying against it, and he has lain there four days when Jesus arrives. At Jesus' command the stone is taken away, and Lazarus comes out at his call.

l: Jesus' raising of Lazarus, The Gospel According to John
s: Jesus has the stone taken away, prays aloud so the crowd may believe the Father sent him, and cries with a loud voice, "Lazarus, come out!" The dead man comes out, and many of the Jews who saw it believe in Jesus. The sign also prompts the council to plot his death. The raising of Lazarus from the dead is recalled as a sign that draws crowds to Bethany and to meet Jesus. The multitude who were present testify about it, the Pharisees lament that the world has gone after Jesus, and the chief priests plot to kill Lazarus because many believed on account of him.

l: resurrection, The Gospel According to John
s: Martha affirms she knows Lazarus will rise in the resurrection at the last day. Jesus responds that he himself is the resurrection and the life, and that whoever believes in him will live even if he dies and will never die. He then demonstrates this by calling Lazarus out of the tomb.

l: ointment (Mary's ointment), The Gospel According to John
s: is_a pure nard [a pound, very precious] The ointment is a pound of pure nard, very precious, which Mary pours on Jesus' feet and which fills the house with fragrance. Judas says it could have been sold for three hundred denarii, while Jesus says she kept it for the day of his burial.

l: crowd (at the feast), The Gospel According to John
s: greets Jesus [with palm branches] A large crowd of the Jews comes to Bethany to see Jesus and Lazarus, and a great multitude at the feast greets Jesus in Jerusalem with palm branches and cries of 'Hosanna!' The multitude that had been with him when he raised Lazarus testifies about it, and they go to meet him because they heard of the sign. Later some of the multitude hear the voice from the sky, think it thunder or an angel, and question how the Christ can be 'lifted up'.

l: Jesus' death and glorification, The Gospel According to John
s: is_described_as grain of wheat [dying to bear much fruit] Jesus links his coming death to his burial, to the time for the Son of Man to be glorified, and to the image of a grain of wheat that falls into the earth and dies to bear much fruit. He says his soul is troubled but he came to this time for this cause, and that being lifted up from the earth will draw all people to himself. The narrator says this signified what kind of death he should die, and that the disciples later remembered these things when Jesus was glorified.

l: belief and unbelief in Jesus, The Gospel According to John
s: has_cause Isaiah's prophecy [unbelief fulfills the word of Isaiah] Many of the Jews believe in Jesus because of Lazarus, while the multitude welcomes him as King, but despite his many signs others do not believe, which the narrator ties to Isaiah's words about blinded eyes and hardened hearts. Many rulers believe but do not confess it for fear of the Pharisees and being put out of the synagogue, because they loved men's praise more than God's. Jesus urges belief in the light so people may become children of light, and says that one who rejects him will be judged by the word he spoke on the last day.

l: disciple whom Jesus loved, The Gospel According to John
s: The disciple whom Jesus loved is a witness whose testimony is declared true. He leaned on Jesus' chest at the supper. At the cross, Jesus tells him "Behold, your mother!" and he takes Mary to his own home. He outruns Peter to the tomb, enters, sees the cloths, and believes. On the beach he first recognizes Jesus: "It's the Lord!" A rumor that he would not die is corrected, since Jesus did not say so. He is identified as the one who testifies about and wrote these things.

l: foot washing, The Gospel According to John
s: is_a example [for disciples to follow] Jesus washes the disciples' feet and wipes them with a towel wrapped around his waist. He presents it as an example, saying that if the Lord and Teacher has washed their feet, they ought to wash one another's feet. Peter's resistance prompts Jesus to say that without being washed, one has no part with him.

l: supper, The Gospel According to John
s: occurs_before Passover [the feast] The supper is the setting before the Passover feast in which Jesus rises, washes feet, and later dips bread for Judas. At the table the disciple whom Jesus loved leans against his chest. Some of those present think Jesus' words to Judas concern buying things for the feast or giving to the poor.

l: betrayal of Jesus, The Gospel According to John
s: fulfills Scripture [quoted passage about eating bread and lifting heel] The devil has already put betrayal into the heart of Judas, and Jesus knows who will betray him. Jesus cites Scripture about one who eats bread with him lifting his heel against him, then announces that one of the disciples will betray him. He identifies Judas with the dipped bread, and Judas leaves.

l: new commandment of love, The Gospel According to John
s: is_a commandment [new] Jesus gives a new commandment that the disciples love one another just as he has loved them. He says that by this love everyone will know they are his disciples.

l: Peter's denial prediction, The Gospel According to John
s: When Peter says he will lay down his life for Jesus, Jesus answers by asking whether he will and tells him the rooster won't crow until Peter has denied him three times. This follows Jesus' statement that Peter cannot follow him now but will follow afterwards.

l: Father's house, The Gospel According to John
s: has many homes Jesus says the Father's house has many homes. He is going there to prepare a place for his disciples so that they may be where he is.

l: the way (path to the Father), The Gospel According to John
s: leads_to God the Father [only through Jesus] Jesus tells the disciples they know where he goes and the way, and when Thomas objects, Jesus says he himself is the way, the truth, and the life. He states that no one comes to the Father except through him.

l: commandments, The Gospel According to John
s: are_kept_by disciples (Jesus' followers) [sign of loving Jesus] Jesus says that if the disciples love him they will keep his commandments, and that the one who has and keeps them is the one who loves him. Those who love him will be loved by the Father and by Jesus, who will reveal himself to them. Whoever does not love him does not keep his words, which are the Father's.

l: Jesus's departure and return ('a little while'), The Gospel According to John
s: Jesus's departure and return, called 'a little while', is a brief span in which the disciples will not see him and then will see him again. It is tied to his going to the Father to prepare a place for them, and it benefits them by enabling the Counselor to come. In Chapter 14 he promises to return, not leave them orphans, and speaks beforehand so they believe. In Chapter 16 they misunderstand the phrase, and he explains it through their sorrow turning to joy.

l: fruit (fruit-bearing), The Gospel According to John
s: Fruit is what disciples bear only by remaining in Jesus, the vine; fruitless branches are burned, fruitful ones pruned for more. Much fruit glorifies the Father, proves discipleship, and was appointed to remain.

l: love, The Gospel According to John
s: has_greatest_form laying down one's life for friends Jesus says he loves the disciples as the Father has loved him, and tells them to remain in his love by keeping his commandments. His commandment is that they love one another as he loved them, and he says there is no greater love than laying down one's life for friends.

l: sorrow turned to joy, The Gospel According to John
s: Jesus's teaching to his disciples that their present weeping while the world rejoices will turn into joy. He likens it to a woman forgetting her anguish after childbirth, promises to see them again, and says their joy will be permanent, made full by asking in his name.

l: disciples (those given to Jesus by the Father), The Gospel According to John
s: The disciples are those the Father gave Jesus out of the world. They keep the Father's word, received Jesus' words, and believe the Father sent him. Though not of the world, and hated by it, they remain in it. Jesus prays that they be protected from the evil one, be one, be sanctified in truth, share his joy, and see his glory.

l: future believers (those who will believe through the disciples' word), The Gospel According to John
s: Future believers are those who will come to believe through the disciples' word. Jesus prays for them beyond the disciples, asking that they be one as the Father and Son are one, so the world may believe.

l: glory, The Gospel According to John
s: is_given_by Father (God) [to Jesus] Jesus asks the Father to glorify him so that he may glorify the Father, and to restore the glory he had with the Father before the world existed. He says he is glorified in the disciples and has given them the glory the Father gave him. He desires that they see his glory, which the Father gave him because he loved him before the foundation of the world.

l: unity (oneness of believers with Father and Son), The Gospel According to John
s: Unity is the oneness of believers with the Father and Son, modeled on the Father-Son oneness. In Chapter 17 Jesus prays that the disciples, then all future believers, be one and perfected, so the world may believe the Father sent him.

l: Pilate, The Gospel According to John
s: Pilate is a judge who claims power to release or crucify and says he is not a Jew. When the Jews will not enter the Praetorium, he tells them to judge Jesus by their own law, then questions Jesus about being king and repeatedly finds no basis for a charge. He offers release under the Passover custom, but the crowd chooses Barabbas. He flogs Jesus, grows more afraid at the Son of God claim, yet, pressed about Caesar's friendship, delivers Jesus to be crucified. He writes the cross title, refuses to change it, and permits Joseph to take the body.

l: detachment of soldiers and officers (sent by the chief priests and Pharisees), The Gospel According to John
s: A detachment of soldiers and officers sent by chief priests and Pharisees, led by Judas, arrives armed with lanterns and torches, falls back at Jesus' words, then seizes and binds him.

l: chief priests, The Gospel According to John
s: declares_allegiance_to Caesar [only king] The chief priests and officers shout "Crucify! Crucify!" when they see Jesus. They declare "We have no king but Caesar!" They later ask Pilate to change the title to say Jesus claimed to be King of the Jews, and Pilate refuses.

l: soldiers, The Gospel According to John
s: The soldiers twist a crown of thorns, dress Jesus in purple, mock him as "King of the Jews," and slap him. After crucifying him they divide his garments into four parts and cast lots for the seamless tunic. They break the legs of the two others but find Jesus already dead, so one of them pierces his side with a spear, and blood and water come out.

l: Golgotha, The Gospel According to John
s: Golgotha, Hebrew name for "The Place of a Skull," lies near the city; Jesus is brought there carrying his cross and crucified, and a garden with a new tomb is nearby.

l: cross (Jesus' cross), The Gospel According to John
s: Jesus bears his cross to Golgotha. Pilate's title, "JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS," is placed on it, written in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek. The Jews wish the bodies not to remain on the crosses during the Sabbath.

l: crucifixion of Jesus, The Gospel According to John
s: includes two others crucified with Jesus [one on either side] Jesus is crucified at Golgotha with two others, one on either side and Jesus in the middle. The soldiers divide his garments, and several women and the beloved disciple stand by. He is given vinegar, declares "It is finished," and dies. The others' legs are broken but his are not, and his side is pierced, which the text says fulfills Scripture.

l: Mary Magdalene, The Gospel According to John
s: Mary Magdalene is the first witness of the risen Jesus. She finds the tomb's stone removed, tells Peter and the other disciple, weeps, sees two angels, mistakes Jesus for the gardener until he names her, then announces to the disciples she has seen the Lord.

l: Joseph of Arimathaea, The Gospel According to John
s: Joseph of Arimathaea, a disciple of Jesus secretly for fear of the Jews, asks Pilate for Jesus' body. Pilate gives permission, and Joseph takes the body away. With Nicodemus he binds it in linen cloths with spices and lays it in the tomb.

l: garden tomb, The Gospel According to John
s: A new, never-used tomb in a garden near where Jesus was crucified; because it was close and Preparation Day had come, Jesus is laid there.

l: burial of Jesus, The Gospel According to John
s: After Pilate grants permission, Joseph of Arimathaea and Nicodemus take Jesus' body and bind it in linen cloths with spices, as is the Jewish burial custom. They lay it in the new tomb in the garden near the crucifixion site because of the Preparation Day.

l: tomb (Jesus' tomb), The Gospel According to John
s: Jesus' tomb is found on the first day of the week with its stone taken away. Peter and the other disciple see the linen cloths left lying inside, and Mary later looks in and sees two angels in white, at the head and feet.

l: Jesus' resurrection, The Gospel According to John
s: is_required_by the Scripture [the disciples did not yet understand] The resurrection is shown through the empty tomb, the angels, and Jesus' appearances to Mary Magdalene, to the disciples, and to Thomas. The text notes the disciples did not yet know the Scripture that he must rise from the dead. Jesus says he is ascending to his Father and God, and the chapter states that the signs are written so that readers may believe he is the Christ, the Son of God.

l: net (the disciples' net), The Gospel According to John
s: has_state not torn [despite the many fish] The net is cast on the right side of the boat at Jesus' word and becomes too full of fish to draw in. The disciples drag it to land, and Peter pulls it ashore holding one hundred fifty-three great fish, yet it is not torn.

l: fish (the great catch), The Gospel According to John
s: has_count 153 [great fish] The fish fill the net so completely that the disciples cannot haul it in, and number one hundred fifty-three great fish. Jesus asks for some of them to be brought, while he already has fish laid on a fire of coals.

l: breakfast (Jesus' meal on the beach), The Gospel According to John
s: consists_of bread [with fish] On landing, the disciples find a fire of coals with fish and bread laid on it. Jesus invites them to come and eat, takes the bread and gives it to them, and the fish likewise. None dares ask who he is, knowing it is the Lord, and the conversation with Peter follows after they have eaten.

l: fishing trip (night fishing), The Gospel According to John
s: has_outcome caught nothing [that night] Peter announces he is going fishing, and the others say they will come too, so they enter the boat. They catch nothing that night, until Jesus' instruction at daybreak changes the outcome.

l: Jesus' appearance to the disciples, The Gospel According to John
s: has_ordinal third [appearance after resurrection] Jesus reveals himself at the sea of Tiberias, standing on the beach unrecognized until the large catch prompts recognition. The text counts this as the third time he was revealed to his disciples after rising from the dead.

l: Jesus' questioning of Peter's love, The Gospel According to John
s: has_count three [asked three times] After breakfast Jesus asks Simon, son of Jonah, three times whether he loves him, the first time adding "more than these." Peter answers each time that Jesus knows he has affection for him, and is grieved at the third asking. Each answer is met with a charge: feed my lambs, tend my sheep, feed my sheep.

l: Peter's future death, The Gospel According to John
s: Jesus foretells Peter's death: once self-dressed and free-walking, in old age Peter will stretch out his hands and be dressed and carried unwillingly by another, signifying a death glorifying God, then Jesus says "Follow me."

l: 1 John
s: This document is John's First Letter, a five-chapter pastoral epistle in which the author writes to his readers, addressing them as little children, to ground them in fellowship with God, the Father, and Jesus Christ, his Son. It opens with the authors' testimony to what they heard, saw, and touched of the Word of life, and announces the central message that God is light with no darkness in him. Walking in the light brings fellowship and the cleansing blood of Jesus; denying sin is self-deception, while confessing sins brings forgiveness from the faithful and righteous God. Chapter 2 presents Jesus Christ as the righteous Counselor and atoning sacrifice for the whole world. Knowing him means keeping his commandments, above all loving one's brother. The readers are told not to love the passing world and are warned about antichrists who deny that Jesus is the Christ, and they are urged to let what they heard from the beginning and the anointing remain in them. Chapter 3 calls believers children of God who will be like him when he is revealed. It contrasts righteousness with sin, which belongs to the devil, and shows love through Cain's murder of his brother as the counterexample and through laying down one's life and helping a brother in need. It ends with confidence before God and the command to believe in his Son and love one another, with the Spirit as the sign that he remains in us. Chapter 4 urges testing spirits, with confession that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh as the test, and grounds love in God's nature, shown by sending his only born Son. Perfect love casts out fear, and claiming to love God while hating a brother is a lie. Chapter 5 teaches that believing Jesus is the Christ means being born of God, and that faith overcomes the world. The Spirit, the water, and the blood agree in testifying that God gave eternal life in his Son. The letter closes with confident prayer according to God's will, remarks on sin that does and does not lead to death, and a warning to keep from idols.

l: God, 1 John
s: God is presented across these records as light with no darkness in him, and as love itself. He is the Father of Jesus Christ, his only born Son, whom he sent into the world so that believers might live through him. The records open with God declared as light, faithful and righteous, forgiving and cleansing those who confess sins; claiming sinlessness makes him a liar. Next, loving the world excludes the Father's love, and confessing the Son means having the Father. He then gives great love so believers are called his children; he is greater than the heart and knows all things. His commandment is to believe in his Son's name and love one another. He loved believers first, remains in those who love one another, and gives them his Spirit as the sign of this. Though no one has ever seen him, he is known through this love. The records close with his testimony about his Son, greater than human witness, his gift of eternal life in the Son, and his listening to those who ask according to his will. Rejecting his testimony makes him a liar.

l: Jesus Christ, 1 John
s: Jesus Christ is the central figure of the 1 John records, presented as the Son of God and the Son of the Father, with whom believers have fellowship. He is righteous, pure, and without sin, and acts as Counselor with the Father. His blood cleanses those who walk in the light, and he is the atoning sacrifice for the sins of the readers and of the whole world. The account unfolds across five chapters. Early on he is the righteous Counselor and example: those who remain in him ought to walk as he walked, and denying that he is the Christ marks the Antichrist. He was then revealed to take away sins and destroy the devil's works, and he laid down his life for us. Next, confessing that he came in the flesh is the test of a spirit being of God; the Father sent him as Savior of the world. Finally, he is declared the Son of God, who came by water and blood, not water only. Belief in him means being born of God, God's testimony is that eternal life is in him, and he is called the true God and eternal life.

l: eternal life, 1 John
s: Eternal life is the life that existed from the beginning with the Father, was revealed to the authors, and was heard, seen and touched. God gave it to believers, and it is in his Son, Jesus Christ: whoever has the Son has the life. It was written so believers may know they have it.

l: authors (the writers of the letter), 1 John
s: The authors of the letter are a group of witnesses who heard, saw, and touched the Word of life. They have fellowship with God, his Son, and Jesus Christ, declare what they witnessed to readers so they may share fellowship, and include themselves in statements on sin.

l: children of God, 1 John
s: The children of God are believers addressed across the records of 1 John. They are called children by the Father's love, born of God, and do not commit sin because his seed remains in them. The account begins with the authors offering fellowship with the Father and the Son and the message that God is light, contrasting walking in light with darkness. It then says they are now God's children and will be like him when he is revealed, are known by doing righteousness and loving their brothers, and are not known by the world. Next they are told to test the spirits, having overcome false prophets because the one in them is greater, and to love one another, remaining in God through his Spirit with boldness for judgment. It ends by saying they are known by loving God and keeping his commandments, and the evil one does not touch them.

l: fellowship, 1 John
s: is_offered_to readers (recipients of the letter) [fellowship with the authors] Fellowship is the purpose of the authors' declaration: that the readers may share it with them, and that it is with the Father and his Son, Jesus Christ. Claiming fellowship with God while walking in darkness is a lie, whereas walking in the light brings fellowship with one another.

l: light, 1 John
s: is_attribute_of God Light is what God is, and walking in it as he is in the light brings fellowship with one another and cleansing by the blood of Jesus Christ from all sin.

l: light and darkness, 1 John
s: is_absent_from God There is no darkness at all in God. Those who say they have fellowship with him yet walk in darkness lie and do not tell the truth.

l: sin, 1 John
s: Sin is lawlessness and includes all unrighteousness.
