The letter first says denying sin is self-deception and makes God a liar, while confessing it brings God's forgiveness and cleansing through the blood of Jesus Christ. It then says whoever sins has not seen or known him, those born of God do not sin because his seed remains, and the Son was revealed to take sins away. Finally it distinguishes sin leading to death from sin not leading to death, for which one should ask and God gives life.

l: little children (the readers), 1 John
s: The readers, addressed as little children, are forgiven for his name's sake, know the Father, have anointing from the Holy One, knowledge, and have overcome the evil one. They are urged not to love the world, to keep what they heard from the beginning, and to remain in him, despite those who would lead them astray.

l: Antichrist, 1 John
s: Antichrist is a spirit and liar already present in the world, denying that Jesus is the Christ and denying the Father and the Son. Many antichrists have arisen, signaling the final hour. They came out of the readers' community without belonging to it, and their departure exposed this.

l: the world, 1 John
s: The world is presented as a moral realm opposed to the Father: it contains the lust of the flesh, lust of the eyes, and pride of life, did not know God's children because it did not know him, may hate believers, and is passing away with its lusts, while God's doer endures forever.

l: commandment, 1 John
s: The commandment is described as both old, the word heard from the beginning, and new, true in him and in the readers as darkness passes and true light shines. Keeping it shows one knows him; claiming to know him without keeping it makes one a liar; keepers have God's love perfected.

l: love and hate of brother, 1 John
s: A contrast between loving and hating one's brother: whoever claims to be in the light yet hates his brother remains blind in darkness, not knowing his direction, while whoever loves his brother remains in the light without stumbling.

l: the devil, 1 John
s: has_been_doing sin [from the beginning] The devil has been sinning from the beginning, and whoever sins is of the devil. The Son of God was revealed to destroy his works, and those who do not do righteousness or love their brother are marked as his children.

l: love, 1 John
s: is_known_by Jesus Christ laying down his life [for us] Love for one another is the message heard from the beginning and a sign of having passed from death into life, while hating a brother is likened to murder, as in Cain's killing of his brother. Love is known through Christ laying down his life, and it must be shown in deed and truth, including by sharing the world's goods with a brother in need.

l: false prophets, 1 John
s: False prophets have gone out into the world carrying the spirit of the Antichrist, already present. They deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, belong to the world, speak its language, and the world listens to them.

l: love, 1 John
s: Love originates from God; those who love are born of God and know him. God's love appeared in sending his Son, perfect love casts out fear, and loving God requires loving one's brother, commanded.

l: commandments of God, 1 John
s: God's commandments are defined as the way of loving God; keeping them shows love for God's children, and they are not grievous.

l: faith, 1 John
s: is victory over the world Faith is named as the victory that has overcome the world. Whatever is born of God overcomes the world, and the one who overcomes is he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God.

l: testimony, 1 John
s: content eternal life in the Son [God's testimony concerning his Son] Three testify: the Spirit, the water, and the blood, and the three agree as one. The Spirit testifies because the Spirit is the truth. God's testimony is that he gave eternal life in his Son, and the one who believes has this testimony in himself.

l: believers, 1 John
s: Believers are those who believe in the name of the Son of God. Born of God and holding testimony in themselves, they are assured of eternal life, keep believing, and have boldness that God hears requests per his will. They know they are of God, and are urged to avoid idols.

l: 2 John
s: In 2 John 1, the elder writes to the chosen lady and her children, whom he loves in truth along with all who know the truth. He wishes them grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Jesus Christ, and rejoices that some of her children walk in truth. He urges them to love one another and to walk according to the commandment they have had from the beginning. He warns that many deceivers, who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, have gone out into the world, and that those who do not remain in the teaching of Christ do not have God. He tells her not to welcome anyone who does not bring this teaching, and says he hopes to visit face to face, closing with greetings from the children of her chosen sister.

l: The elder, 2 John
s: The elder writes to the chosen lady and her children, whom he loves in truth. He rejoices that some of her children walk in truth, begs her to love one another, warns against deceivers, and hopes to visit and speak face to face so their joy may be full.

l: chosen lady (the elder's addressee), 2 John
s: The chosen lady is addressed by the elder as the recipient of the letter and is begged to love one another. She is instructed not to receive into her house or welcome anyone who does not bring the teaching, since welcoming such a person means sharing in his evil deeds.

l: children (the chosen lady's children), 2 John
s: The chosen lady's children are loved by the elder in truth, and he rejoices that he has found some of them walking in truth as commanded by the Father. The children of her chosen sister send greetings at the end of the letter.

l: God the Father, 2 John
s: God the Father is named as a source of grace, mercy, and peace, together with Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father. He is the one who commanded that they walk in truth, and whoever remains in the teaching has both the Father and the Son.

l: Jesus Christ, 2 John
s: Jesus Christ is called the Lord and the Son of the Father, and is a source of grace, mercy, and peace. Deceivers are identified by their refusal to confess that he came in the flesh, and whoever remains in his teaching has both the Father and the Son.

l: truth, 2 John
s: Truth is the basis of the elder's love for the lady and her children, and is known by all who share that love. It remains in them and will be with them forever, and some of the children are found walking in it.

l: love, 2 John
s: Love is the subject of the commandment the elder urges, that they love one another. It is defined as walking according to God's commandments, and grace, mercy, and peace are with them in truth and love.

l: commandment, 2 John
s: The commandment is described as not new but what they have had from the beginning, that they love one another. It is explained that love means walking according to his commandments, and that they should walk in it as they heard from the beginning.

l: deceivers, 2 John
s: Deceivers are said to have gone out into the world in large numbers, and are those who do not confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. They are called the deceiver and the Antichrist, and anyone who welcomes one shares in his evil deeds.

l: teaching of Christ, 2 John
s: The teaching of Christ is the standard by which people are judged: whoever transgresses and does not remain in it does not have God, while whoever remains in it has both the Father and the Son. Anyone who comes without bringing this teaching is not to be received or welcomed.

l: 3 John
s: In 3 John, the elder (John) writes to Gaius, whom he loves, praising him for walking in the truth and for his faithful work toward brothers and strangers. He urges Gaius to send traveling brothers on their way in a manner worthy of God, since they went out for the sake of the Name and took nothing from the Gentiles. He criticizes Diotrephes, who loves to be first, rejects the elder's words, accuses him with wicked words, refuses to receive the brothers, and expels those who would. He commends Demetrius as having a good testimony from all and from the truth itself, and says he hopes to visit Gaius soon to speak face to face.

l: John, 3 John
s: Writing as the elder, John addresses Gaius with love, prays for his prosperity and health, and says he has no greater joy than hearing his children walk in truth. He says he wrote to the assembly, plans to call attention to Diotrephes's deeds if he comes, vouches for Demetrius, and hopes to see Gaius soon rather than write more with ink and pen.

l: Gaius, 3 John
s: Gaius is the beloved recipient of the letter, praised because brothers testified to his walking in truth and to his love before the assembly. He is told he does a faithful work for brothers and strangers, is urged to send them forward worthily and to imitate good rather than evil, and is told John hopes to see him soon.

l: Diotrephes, 3 John
s: Diotrephes is described as one who loves to be first among the assembly and does not accept what John and his companions say. He unjustly accuses them with wicked words, refuses to receive the brothers, and forbids and throws out of the assembly those who would; John says he will call attention to these deeds if he comes.

l: Demetrius, 3 John
s: Demetrius is said to have the testimony of all and of the truth itself. John adds that he and his companions also testify for him, and that their testimony is true.

l: brothers (traveling believers), 3 John
s: Brothers came and testified about Gaius's truth and love before the assembly. They went out for the sake of the Name, taking nothing from the Gentiles, and John says they ought to be received and sent on their journey worthily; Diotrephes refuses to receive them.

l: truth, 3 John
s: Truth is the standard by which John rejoices in Gaius, who walks in truth, and he has no greater joy than hearing his children walk in it. Receiving the traveling brothers makes believers fellow workers for the truth, and Demetrius has the testimony of the truth itself.

l: hospitality toward traveling brothers, 3 John
s: John commends Gaius for his faithful work and love toward brothers and strangers and urges him to send them forward in a way worthy of God. He says such people ought to be received so that believers may be fellow workers for the truth, in contrast to Diotrephes, who refuses them and expels those who welcome them.

l: Revelation
s: This document is the book of Revelation, twenty-two chapters presented as a vision given by God to Jesus Christ and shown through his angel to John, who writes it for seven assemblies in Asia. The central figures are Jesus, the Lamb who was slain and the Living one holding the keys of Death and Hades; God on the throne; and John, the narrator. Opposing them are the dragon (the old serpent, the devil and Satan), the beast from the sea, the second beast or false prophet, and the great prostitute called Babylon. Chapter 1 opens with John on Patmos seeing one like a son of man among seven golden lamp stands. Chapters 2 and 3 are seven letters to the assemblies (Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea), each praising or rebuking and ending with a promise to the one who overcomes. Chapters 4 and 5 move to heaven, with the throne, twenty-four elders, four living creatures, and a sealed scroll that only the Lamb can open. Chapters 6 to 9 and 11 follow the opening of seven seals and the sounding of seven trumpets, bringing conquest, war, famine, death, cosmic upheaval, and plagues, interrupted in chapter 7 by the sealing of 144,000 and a countless multitude in white robes. Chapter 10 gives John a little book to eat, and chapter 11 describes two witnesses, killed and raised, and the kingdom of the world becoming the Lord's. Chapters 12 to 14 portray the woman, the child, the dragon's war and fall, the two beasts, the mark and the number 666, the Lamb with the 144,000, three angels' proclamations, and a harvest of wrath. Chapters 15 and 16 present seven bowls of God's wrath ending at Harmagedon with "It is done!" Chapters 17 and 18 show the prostitute's destruction and Babylon's fall and mourning by kings and merchants. Chapter 19 celebrates the Lamb's wedding and shows the white-horse rider, the Word of God, defeating the beast and false prophet. Chapter 20 binds Satan for a thousand years, describes the saints' reign, Satan's final defeat, and the judgment before the great white throne. Chapters 21 and 22 close with a new heaven and earth, New Jerusalem, the river and tree of life, God dwelling with people and wiping away tears, a warning not to alter the book, Jesus's promise to come soon, and the prayer "Come, Lord Jesus."

l: Christ, Revelation
s: Christ, called Jesus Christ, is portrayed in Revelation as the faithful witness, firstborn of the dead, and ruler of the kings of the earth, who loves his people, washed them from sins by his blood, and made them a Kingdom and priests. He is the first and the last, the Living one who was dead and is alive forever, holding the keys of Death and Hades and seven stars in his right hand. In Chapter 1 he is seen as a son of man among lamp stands, coming with the clouds. In Chapter 11 he is the crucified Lord of the two witnesses, and heaven declares the world's kingdom has become his, reigning forever. In Chapter 14, crowned in gold on a white cloud, he reaps the earth with a sharp sickle. In Chapter 20 the faithful live and reign with him for a thousand years as priests.

l: God, Revelation
s: God, in these records, is the Almighty, the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End, the one who is, was and is to come. He is the living God who lives forever and ever, sits on the throne with seven Spirits before it, and created heaven, earth, sea and everything in them. He is holy, the only holy one, King of the nations, Lord, and strong. His ways are righteous and true, and his judgments are true and righteous. He holds power over the plagues, and Christ has authority from him. The account opens with God giving the Revelation to Jesus Christ to show his servants what must happen soon, and sending his angel to do so. Grace and peace come from him, and believers are made priests to him. He is called Father and God of overcomers, and the overcomer is promised a place as a pillar in his temple, with his name and the name of his city, the new Jerusalem, written on them. The middle chapters show God enthroned and worshiped by multitudes, angels, elders and living creatures with blessing, glory, wisdom, honor, power and might. He seals his bondservants, gives power to his two witnesses and raises them, prepares a wilderness place for the woman, and receives her child. His salvation, power and Kingdom come together with the authority of his Christ. The beast blasphemes his name, and people refuse to repent under the plagues. His wrath is prepared as unmixed wine, trodden in the great wine press. He remembers Babylon the great and judges her, and heaven rejoices. He sends fire from heaven that devours the nations surrounding the saints' camp. Those in the first resurrection become his priests. The records end with restoration. God dwells with people in the New Jerusalem, wipes away every tear, and ends death, mourning, crying and pain. He declares he is making all things new, offers the water of life to the thirsty, and promises that the overcomer will be his son. He and the Lamb are the city's temple, his glory is its light, and he will illuminate his people so there is no night. He is the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets. The angel directs John to worship God alone, and God warns that he will add plagues to anyone who adds to the book's words, and take away the share of anyone who removes from them.

l: John, Revelation
s: John is a servant of Jesus Christ and the narrator-witness of the Revelation, writing to seven assemblies as their brother and partner in oppression, Kingdom, and perseverance in Christ Jesus. He testifies to God's word and the testimony of Jesus Christ about all he saw, and he was on the isle of Patmos because of God's Word. What matters most is his role as the one who heard and saw the visions and is commissioned to record them. The records unfold in sequence. In chapter 1, in the Spirit on the Lord's day, he hears a voice and sees one like a son of man, falls as dead, is comforted, and is told to write what he has seen, what is, and what will happen hereafter. In chapter 4 he sees a door opened in heaven, is called up, and is immediately in the Spirit, describing the throne, elders, and living creatures. In chapter 5 he weeps because no one is worthy to open the sealed book, until an elder consoles him and the Lamb appears amid universal worship. In chapter 7 he sees the sealed and the great multitude, answering an elder, 'My lord, you know,' and receiving the explanation. In chapter 10 he is forbidden to write what the seven thunders said, eats the little book, finding it sweet and bitter, and is told he must prophesy again over many peoples, nations, languages, and kings. In chapter 17 he is carried in the Spirit into a wilderness, marvels at the woman on the beast, and an angel interprets. In chapter 21 he sees the new heaven and earth and the holy city, is told to write, and is carried to a high mountain to see the city measured. In chapter 22 he identifies himself as the one who heard and saw these things, is stopped from worshiping before the angel, is told not to seal the prophecy, and ends with the cry, 'Yes, come, Lord Jesus!'

l: seven assemblies, Revelation
s: The seven assemblies in Asia (Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea) receive John's greeting and book. Represented by seven golden lamp stands, their angels are the seven stars in Christ's right hand.

l: Revelation, Revelation
s: Revelation is a prophecy given by God to Jesus Christ, conveyed through his angel to John, showing servants what must happen soon. It blesses those who read, hear, and keep it, then commands John to write it down and send it to seven assemblies.

l: servants of God, Revelation
s: God's servants serve him in the holy city, see his face, bear his name on their foreheads, and reign forever with the Lord God as light; the angel calls himself their fellow bondservant.

l: Death, Revelation
s: Death is the rider on the pale horse in Chapter 6, followed by Hades, and is given authority over one fourth of the earth to kill by sword, famine, death, and wild animals.

l: Jesus, Revelation
s: Jesus is presented as the exalted Son of God who speaks to seven assemblies and is described with striking imagery: he holds seven stars in his right hand, walks among seven golden lamp stands, has eyes like fire, feet like burnished brass, and a sharp two-edged sword. In chapters 2 and 3 he addresses each assembly under a different description, such as the first and last who was dead and came to life, the holy and true one with the key of David, and the Faithful and True Witness, the Beginning of God's creation. He claims to know their works and to search minds and hearts. He praises Philadelphia, which he loves and keeps from the hour of testing, rebukes Sardis and Laodicea, reproves and chastens those he loves, threatens judgment on Jezebel and her followers, and promises rewards to overcomers. He stands at the door and knocks, promising to dine with whoever opens, and promises a seat on his throne as he sat with his Father on his throne, having received authority from his Father. In chapter 21 he appears as the Lamb, husband of the bride, the city's wife. The city's foundations bear the names of his twelve Apostles, he is with the Lord God the Almighty its temple and lamp, and his book of life lists who may enter. In chapter 22 he declares he is coming soon with his reward to repay each according to his work, calls himself the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End, the root and offspring of David, and the Bright and Morning Star, says he sent his angel to testify to the assemblies, and the text closes with grace for all the saints.

l: Ephesus assembly, Revelation
s: The Ephesus assembly is commended for its works, toil, perseverance, rejecting evil men, exposing false apostles, and hating the Nicolaitans' works, but rebuked for leaving its first love, and told to remember, repent, and return, or lose its lamp stand.

l: Smyrna assembly, Revelation
s: Smyrna assembly is a community in poverty yet called rich, blasphemed by a false-Jewish synagogue of Satan. It is told not to fear coming prison testing and ten days of oppression, urged to stay faithful to death for the crown of life, and receives no rebuke.

l: Pergamum assembly, Revelation
s: A community dwelling where Satan's throne is, it holds firmly to Jesus' name and kept its faith even when Antipas, a faithful witness, was killed. Rebuked because some follow Balaam's and the Nicolaitans' teaching, it is told to repent or face war by the sword.

l: Thyatira assembly, Revelation
s: Thyatira assembly is praised for love, faith, service and endurance, with growing works, but rebuked for tolerating Jezebel; the faithful remnant rejecting her teaching bear no extra burden and must hold firm until he comes.

l: Jezebel, Revelation
s: Jezebel is a woman in Thyatira who calls herself a prophetess and seduces the speaker's servants into sexual immorality and eating idol sacrifices. Given time to repent, she refuses. Judgment follows: she and her adulterous followers face great oppression, and her children will be killed with Death.

l: children of Israel, Revelation
s: The children of Israel are a people made up of twelve tribes: Judah, Reuben, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, and Benjamin. From each tribe 12,000 are sealed, totaling 144,000, listed in sequence in Chapter 7.

l: Satan, Revelation
s: Satan is a great red dragon with seven heads, ten horns, and seven crowns, also called the old serpent and the devil. He is the deceiver of the whole world and the accuser of the brothers before God day and night. He is first seen drawing a third of the stars down and threatening the woman's child. Defeated in war, he is thrown down to earth with his angels, furious because his time is short. He persecutes the woman and her offspring, and gives the first beast power, throne, and authority, so people worship him. Finally he is bound in the sealed abyss for the thousand years, then thrown into the lake of fire, tormented forever.

l: the one who overcomes, Revelation
s: The one who overcomes is a recipient of promised rewards given across the letters, spoken by a speaker who addresses each message. Chapter 2 promises eating from the tree of life in Paradise, safety from the second death, hidden manna, a white stone with a new name, authority over the nations to rule with a rod of iron, and the morning star, for those who keep his works to the end. Chapter 3 continues: white garments, a name kept in the book of life and confessed before the Father and his angels, becoming a pillar in God's temple, receiving the names of God and the new Jerusalem, and finally sitting with the speaker on his throne.

l: tree of life, Revelation
s: The tree of life stands in Paradise on both sides of the river of water of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit monthly. Its leaves heal the nations. Those who keep God's commandments have right to it; God removes the share of anyone who removes words from the book.

l: lake of fire, Revelation
s: The lake of fire and sulfur, named the second death, is a place of eternal torment where the devil joins the beast and false prophet, Death and Hades are thrown, and anyone absent from the book of life is cast.

l: sexual immorality and eating idol sacrifices, Revelation
s: These practices are condemned as the fruit of false teaching: Balaam taught Balak to put a stumbling block before Israel in this way, and the same teaching is held by some in Pergamum. In Thyatira, Jezebel leads the speaker's servants into them, and she refuses to repent of her sexual immorality.

l: angel of the assembly in Sardis, Revelation
s: The angel of the assembly in Sardis is the addressee of the first message in this unit, which is written to him. The speaker's words to the assembly come through this angel.

l: assembly in Sardis, Revelation
s: The assembly in Sardis appears alive but is dead, with no works found perfected before God. It is commanded to wake up, strengthen what remains, remember, keep, and repent, or be met like a thief. A few undefiled names will walk in white.

l: angel of the assembly in Philadelphia, Revelation
s: The angel of the assembly in Philadelphia is the addressee of the second message in this unit, which is written to him. The speaker's words to the assembly come through this angel.

l: assembly in Philadelphia, Revelation
s: The assembly in Philadelphia is a church with little power that kept the speaker's word and did not deny his name. He rewards it with an open door no one can shut, humbles those of Satan's synagogue before it, keeps it from the hour of testing, and urges it to hold fast so no one takes its crown.
